subject: Calculating weighted stratum estimates at multiple data levels

messages.author: 9237fe2e8425bbde
messages.subject: Calculating weighted stratum estimates at multiple data levels
parts:
Dear List,

We have some questions regarding structuring and analyzing distance
sampling data for an ongoing study of wintering grassland birds. The
study design is as follows. There are 10 study areas (Grassland
Priority Conservation Areas, or GPCAs) that are widely distributed
inside the study region, which is roughly 1000 x 400 km. Within each of
these GPCAs are a grid of blocks, roughly 18 x 18 km in size. Blocks
were chosen at random within each GPCA and in proportion to the total
number available within each GPCA. Within each block, three random
points along roads were selected. From these three points, two opposing
1 km line-transects were run, perpendicular to the road, by separate
observers. We have three years of data.

Strata are organized as follows:

Region
GPCA
Block - contains area values
Sample - contains transect names and a field "Block-Year" for
post-stratification purposes
Observation

We want to estimate bird density for each GPCA for each of the three
years of the study. In addition, we would like each stratum estimate
for GPCA-Year to be the mean of block density estimates weighted by the
grassland area within each block. We would also like to make use of all
observations from all years for the creation of detection functions.
This allows us a large enough sample size to create a detection function
for several rare and threatened species. Our understanding is that
Distance only uses weighting to combine strata level into a global
density estimate. However, we would like strata level (GPCA) density
estimates that are weighted by grassland area in the blocks. We plan to
use block level density estimates in the SPsurvey package in R
(total.est function) and/or the delta method to calculate weighted GPCA
estimates by year (and associated variances) using the mean of block
estimates weighted by the grassland area within each block. Block
estimates are derived by post-stratifying on a field in the sample layer
that is a combination of Block ID and Year.

The main thought behind doing this that it seems logical that densities
in blocks with more grassland should be given more weight towards a GPCA
average (although there is some uncertainty among staff that this is the
correct course of action). We were also hoping to avoid the use of
multipliers given that we are estimating densities for ~30 species.

1. Is calculating the weighted stratum level estimates outside Distance
our only course of action?
2. Considering the blocks were randomly selected within the GPCAs, is it
necessary to weight the GPCA density estimates by the area of grassland
in the blocks?
3. If the blocks were not selected randomly or were systematically
surveyed, would it then be advisable to weight GPCA density estimates by
the area of grassland in the blocks?

Any help is much appreciated,
Greg
greg.levandoski AT rmbo.org

--

messages.author: 66ccc45d15a7b065
messages.subject: Re: Calculating weighted stratum estimates at multiple data levels
parts:
I'll add one piece of information here which may help -- our goal is not
just to estimate species density in each GPCA, but to estimate the
population size of each species in each GPCA in each year. Because
grassland area in each survey block varies, but survey effort is generally
the same, we felt it might be important to include the proportion of
grassland represented by each block relative to the total area for the GPCA
when developing GPCA-level (and higher level) population estimates. Also,
although we are also interested in processes at the site level (i.e. the
transects), the Blocks are the primary sampling unit.

Cheers,

Arvind Panjabi
Rocky Mountain Bird Observatory

messages.author: a6740baad600e37a
messages.subject: Re: Calculating weighted stratum estimates at multiple data levels
parts:
Hi Greg=2C
Neat questions. It seems to me that an important issue may be buried in yo=
ur comment=2C "If the blocks were not selected randomly or were systematica=
lly surveyed=2C would it then be advisable to weight GPCA density estimates=
by the area of grassland in the blocks". If you have any concern about co=
verage probability (i.e.=2C how to weight survey blocks)=2C and are particu=
larly interested in the role of an environmental covariate=2C then this str=
ikes me as a problem that lends itself inherently to density surface modell=
ing. These methods relax the assumptions about representative coverage=2C =
and just require you to have reasonable coverage across the range of covari=
ates (spatial and environmental=2C in this case). In Arvind's update=2C th=
e goals you both outline ("to estimate the population size of each species =
in each GPCA in each year. Because grassland area in each survey block vari=
es=2C but survey effort is generally the same") describe a spatio-temporal =
model to me. The DSM help files in D6 have good examples. You can easily =
use year as a covariate (factor) and estimate abundance in any sub-area.
=20
If you're married to a conventional distance sampling analysis=2C it seems =
to me that you want to weight strata according to coverage probability=2C n=
ot by some environmental covariate that you chose post-hoc: you didn't inc=
lude it at the design stage. Or am I misunderstanding? Did you choose you=
r blocks based on % grassland cover? Given the situation you describe=2C a=
conventional method could be used to test whether density is indeed higher=
in some blocks than others. If so=2C then use your understanding of the b=
iology (some birds prefer grassland) to discuss why density might have been=
higher in some blocks than others. But it might be more efficient to do a=
model-based estimate -- if you want an abundance estimate by location and =
year=2C DSM methods will give you that=2C while modelling the relationship =
between habitat and abundance directly. =20
=20
Good luck. Sounds as though you have a lot of data to work with and great =
coverage.
=20
Best=2C
Rob Williams
=20
